title: Can a website AI agent answer technical questions before the sales call?
summary: Yes, for lookups your docs already answer. Storylane Buyability Index data on 3,727 technical questions shows where answers live and what to hand off.
body_markdown:
Yes, for most of them. In the Storylane Buyability Index, about two in three technical buyer questions already had a full answer on the company's own public website, and only 19 of 3,727 were held back for sales. The answers usually exist. They sit in docs and help articles that the buyer never reaches, and the job of a website agent is to bring them to the buyer and hand the rest to a sales engineer.


That second part matters as much as the first. Some technical questions really do need a person. Most only sound like they do. I think the useful split is between **lookup questions** , whose answer is a published fact, and **judgement questions** , whose answer depends on the buyer's own setup. An agent should answer every lookup on the spot and route every judgement question with its context attached.


## What counts as a technical question?


The Storylane Buyability Index scanned 529 B2B websites between Sep 8 and Oct 20, 2026. For each company it generated about 20 questions a buyer would plausibly ask, 10,580 in all, tagged each one by the buyer role likely to ask it, and then searched the public site for an answer. Two caveats belong next to every number below: the questions are generated per company, not logged from real buyers, and the 529 sites were chosen by the people who ran the scans.


3,727 of the 10,580 questions (35.2%) were tagged as ones a technical evaluator would ask, and they came up on 524 of the 529 sites. They look like this: "Can we deploy this fully on-premises, or is it SaaS only?" "Where is our company data physically stored and hosted?" "How deep is the CRM integration?"


Here is how the public websites did on them.


Technical questions, by topic Questions Fully answered on the site Partly answered


Product and features 816 76.2% 21.6%


Integrations 1,003 71.3% 23.3%


Security 759 57.6% 36.2%


Implementation 588 51.2% 43.2%


All technical questions 3,727 63.8% 30.9%


Source: the Storylane Buyability Index, technical-evaluator questions only. The table shows the four largest topics; the total includes smaller ones. Of all 3,727, 4.8% had no answer anywhere on the site, and 0.5% were gated or sent to sales on purpose.


That last number is the surprise. Companies are not hiding technical answers for the sales call. On 95% of these questions, a full or partial answer is already public.


## Why do buyers save technical questions for the call?


If the answers are public, you would expect buyers to find them. The data on what buyers actually ask says they don't even try. In Storylane's[Modern Buying Trends 2026 analysis](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-buyer-journey-statistics) , integration and data questions made up 16.5% of the 26,382 questions buyers asked RepX across 19 website deployments, and 29.7% of the 5,687 prospect questions on 402 human discovery calls. Implementation showed the same tilt: 9.2% against 13.1%. Buyers ask an agent about price and take integrations to a person almost twice as often.


The obvious explanation is that technical answers need an expert. That fits some questions. It doesn't fit most of the ones in the Index, because most of them have a published answer that no expert needs to interpret.


I have a theory for why buyers route them to a person anyway. Technical questions are phrased about the buyer's own world. "Do you support SSO with *our* identity provider?" sounds like it needs someone who understands our setup. In the Index, 1,468 of the technical questions (39.4%) were phrased around "our", "we" or "us". Those questions were fully answered on the public site 65.1% of the time, slightly more often than technical questions overall. The wording makes a lookup sound like a judgement call, so the buyer waits for a call to ask it.


That is the cost. A question a docs page could answer becomes a reason to wait for a meeting.


## Lookup questions and judgement questions


Sort every technical question by one test: could the answer be written down once and be true for every buyer who asks?


- **Lookup questions** pass the test. Do you support SAML SSO? Which regions can data be hosted in? Is there a REST API, and is it on every plan? Does the integration sync both ways? These have one right answer, and it usually already lives in your docs, trust centre or help centre.
- **Judgement questions** fail it. Will this work with our custom-built CRM objects? How long would rollout take across our 14 business units? Can you sign our data processing addendum with our changes? The answer depends on facts about the buyer, or it commits your company to something.


The examples above are illustrative, not counted. The point is the test. A lookup question answered by a person is a waste of that person. A judgement question answered by an agent is a risk. The skill is telling them apart, and that is something you decide once, in setup, not in every chat.


The Index suggests most technical questions are lookups. 63.8% already had a full published answer, which is exactly what a lookup is. And the companies themselves gated only 0.5% as "talk to us" material.


## Where do the answers to technical questions live?


Mostly far from where buyers start. Of the 2,377 technical questions the Index found a full answer for, 18.5% were answered on docs or developer pages, 15.4% in the help centre or FAQ, and 12.7% on the blog or resources. Together that is 46.5%. The homepage answered 27 of them, or 1.1%. Product and feature pages answered 9.3%.


We have written about this pattern across all buyer questions in[why most B2B websites answer buyer questions in the docs, not on the homepage](https://www.storylane.io/blog/website-answers-hidden-in-docs) , and about why the high-stakes questions get thinner answers in[the assurance gap](https://www.storylane.io/blog/b2b-website-assurance-gap) . For technical questions the consequence is specific. A technical evaluator lands on a marketing page, sees "enterprise-grade security" and "integrates with your stack", and has to guess whether the docs hold more. Many don't look. They add the question to the list for the call.


An agent changes the distance, not the content. It reads the docs page so the buyer doesn't have to find it, and it answers on the page where the question came up.


## Which technical questions should go to a sales engineer?


Give your agent a short, explicit list of questions it hands off. I would start with these five kinds:


1. **Custom architecture.** Anything that depends on the buyer's own data model, custom objects or in-house systems.
2. **Scale and performance for their case.** Their data volumes, their user counts, their peak loads.
3. **Contract changes.** Edits to security terms, data processing agreements or SLAs.
4. **Roadmap.** Anything that asks you to promise a future capability or a date.
5. **Exceptions.** "We know you don't usually do this, but could you?"


Everything outside that list is fair game for the agent, as long as it can point to the page its answer came from. A handoff is not a failure either. A judgement question that arrives at the sales engineer with the buyer's setup already written down lets the call skip straight past discovery. If you run presales,[the technical win checklist for sales engineers](https://www.storylane.io/blog/technical-win) covers what that call should then prove.


## How do you set up a website agent to answer technical questions?


This is where I should say that we sell a website agent, RepX, so weigh this section with that in mind. The steps below work whichever agent you run.


1. **Collect 30 real technical questions.** Pull them from sales call notes, your chat transcripts and your sales engineers' heads. Add the generated list from a Buyability scan if you have one.
2. **Sort them into lookup and judgement.** Use the one test above. Expect most to be lookups.
3. **Find the page that answers each lookup.** If the answer only exists in an engineer's memory, write the help article first. The agent can only bring the buyer an answer that has been written down somewhere.
4. **Give the agent those pages.** Docs, help centre, trust and security pages, integration pages, and the call scripts your best sales engineers use. Then ask it the 30 questions yourself and check every answer against its source.
5. **Write the handoff rule.** List the judgement types, and tell the agent to collect the buyer's context before it routes them.
6. **Read the transcripts every week.** New technical questions show up in chat before they show up anywhere else. Each one is either a new help article or a new line in the handoff rule.


RepX is built for teams in exactly this position: good technical answers already published, a long way from the pages buyers land on. According to[the RepX page](https://www.storylane.io/repx) (checked Oct 30, 2026), you feed it your docs, website, decks, call scripts and interactive demos, and it presents the right asset at the right point in the conversation. It also pulls up a relevant interactive demo when the buyer wants to see how something works. Qualified leads and conversation summaries flow to HubSpot, Salesforce and Slack, so the sales engineer sees the question and the context before the call. On the same page, Hospitable's product marketing manager says RepX "answers very specific product questions" (more in their[customer story](https://www.storylane.io/customer-stories/how-hospitable-booked-36-meetings-in-a-month-with-repx) ).


Technical questions are not a side topic in these conversations. In a hand-coded sample of RepX conversations (2,225 question messages from five deployments, internal Storylane data), integrations and ecosystem was the third most common topic at 9.9%, behind only pricing and feature checks. More on that sample in[five learnings from RepX conversations](https://www.storylane.io/blog/5-learnings-from-1-332-repx-conversations-and-what-they-mean-for-your-own-ai-sdr) .


## What to do this week


The idea to keep is the split. **Most technical questions are lookups that sound like judgement calls, and an agent should answer every lookup and route every judgement question with its context attached.**


On Monday, ask one sales engineer for the ten technical questions they answer most often on first calls. For each, find the public page that answers it. The ones with a page are questions your website could have answered before the call. The ones without a page are your next ten help articles.
